h81.content:
Pope Boniface VIII proclaimed the first Jubilee, or Holy Year, in 1300, granting a special indulgence to pilgrims who visited the basilicas of Sts. Peter and Paul in Rome. Enormous crowds came from across Europe.

Jubilees have been celebrated since then, now ordinarily every 25 years. They are times of pilgrimage, conversion, and mercy, marked by the opening of the Holy Doors.

h82.content:
Bubonic plague swept across Europe and killed perhaps a third to a half of the population in just a few years. Many priests, friars, and nuns died while caring for the sick and burying the dead.

When mobs blamed Jews for the plague, Pope Clement VI issued bulls in 1348 condemning the accusation and forbidding violence against them. The catastrophe left deep marks on piety and art, including a new focus on death, judgment, and Christ’s Passion.

h83.content:
A teenage peasant girl who said she was guided by the voices of Sts. Michael, Catherine, and Margaret, Joan led French forces to lift the siege of Orléans in 1429 and saw Charles VII crowned at Reims.

Captured by the Burgundians and handed to the English, she was condemned by a politically motivated church court and burned at the stake in 1431 at nineteen. A papal retrial declared her innocent in 1456, and she was canonized in 1920.

h84.content:
On May 29, 1453, after a long siege, the Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II captured Constantinople, ending the Byzantine Empire after more than a thousand years. The great church of Hagia Sophia was turned into a mosque.

The city’s fall ended the short-lived union agreed at the Council of Florence and sent Greek scholars and manuscripts westward, helping to fuel the Renaissance.

h85.content:
Johannes Gutenberg’s press in Mainz produced the first major book printed with movable type in Europe: a two-volume Latin Vulgate Bible. About 180 copies were made, and roughly 49 survive today, in whole or in part.

Printing made books, including the Scriptures, catechisms, and devotional works, far more widely available than ever before, transforming the Church and European culture.

h86.content:
One of the first Jesuits, St. Francis Xavier arrived in Goa, India, in 1542. Over the next decade he preached in India, the Malay Peninsula, and the Moluccas, and in 1549 he became one of the first Christian missionaries to reach Japan.

He died in 1552 on Shangchuan Island, within sight of the China he hoped to evangelize. He is patron of the missions.

h87.content:
Carrying out a decision of the Council of Trent, Pope St. Pius V published a revised Roman Missal in 1570 with the bull Quo Primum. It standardized the celebration of Mass throughout most of the Latin Church.

This form of the Mass was used for four centuries, until the Missal of Pope St. Paul VI was promulgated in 1969, following the Second Vatican Council. Today it is often called the Traditional Latin Mass.

h88.content:
The Julian calendar had drifted ten days out of step with the seasons, which affected the date of Easter. Pope Gregory XIII, drawing on the work of Aloysius Lilius and the Jesuit astronomer Christopher Clavius, reformed the calendar in 1582: Thursday, October 4 was followed by Friday, October 15.

Catholic countries adopted it at once. It is now the civil calendar used around the world.

h89.content:
The Italian Jesuit Matteo Ricci arrived in Macau in 1582 and spent nearly three decades in China. He mastered Chinese, dressed as a scholar, shared European mathematics and astronomy, and presented the faith in terms of Chinese culture.

In 1601 he was allowed to settle in Beijing, where he died in 1610, the first foreigner granted a burial plot by the emperor. Pope Francis declared him Venerable in 2022.

h90.content:
Beginning in 1609, Jesuit missionaries organized the Guaraní people into self-governing mission towns, or "reductions," in what is now Paraguay, Argentina, and Brazil. The towns protected the Guaraní from slave raiders and forced labor, and were known for their churches, music, and craftsmanship.

The reductions ended when the Spanish crown expelled the Jesuits in 1767. Their story is told in the 1986 film The Mission.

h91.content:
Pope Gregory XV founded the Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith (Propaganda Fide) to coordinate the Church’s worldwide missions. It trained native clergy, sent missionaries, and freed missions from dependence on colonial powers.

It was renamed the Congregation for the Evangelization of Peoples in 1967 and became part of the Dicastery for Evangelization in 2022.

h92.content:
After German unification, Chancellor Otto von Bismarck launched a "culture struggle" against the Catholic Church. Laws expelled the Jesuits, put seminaries and clergy under state control, and imprisoned or exiled bishops and priests. At its height, many parishes were left without pastors.

Catholics resisted peacefully and organized politically through the Centre Party. Under Pope Leo XIII, most of the laws were repealed in the late 1870s and 1880s.

h93.content:
During the Spanish Civil War, thousands of Catholics were killed out of hatred for the faith. Among them were 13 bishops, more than 4,000 diocesan priests, over 2,000 religious brothers and priests, and nearly 300 religious sisters, along with many laypeople. Churches and monasteries across Spain were burned.

Well over a thousand of these martyrs have since been beatified, including 498 in a single ceremony in 2007 and 522 in 2013.

h94.content:
In January 1964, Pope St. Paul VI and Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras met in Jerusalem, the first meeting of a pope and patriarch of Constantinople in more than five centuries. On December 7, 1965, the day before the Second Vatican Council closed, they jointly lifted the mutual excommunications of 1054.

The act did not end the schism, but it opened a new era of dialogue and friendship between Catholics and Orthodox that continues today.

h95.content:
Pope St. John Paul II invited young people to Rome for Palm Sunday during the Holy Year of 1984 and the International Year of Youth in 1985. The first World Youth Day was celebrated in dioceses in 1986, and the first international gathering took place in Buenos Aires in 1987.

World Youth Days have since drawn millions, including an estimated four to five million people to the closing Mass in Manila in 1995.

h96.content:
Pope St. John Paul II opened the Holy Door of St. Peter’s on Christmas Eve 1999 to begin the Great Jubilee marking two thousand years since the birth of Christ. Millions of pilgrims came to Rome.

On March 12, 2000, the Day of Pardon, the Pope asked God’s forgiveness for sins committed by Christians throughout history. Later that month he made a historic pilgrimage to the Holy Land. The Jubilee closed on the Epiphany, January 6, 2001.

h97.content:
On Divine Mercy Sunday, April 27, 2014, Pope Francis canonized two of his predecessors, Pope St. John XXIII and Pope St. John Paul II, in St. Peter’s Square. Pope Emeritus Benedict XVI was present, so four popes were involved in a single celebration.

John XXIII had called the Second Vatican Council, and John Paul II had led the Church for nearly 27 years.

h98.content:
On April 15, 2019, Monday of Holy Week, fire broke out in the roof of Notre-Dame de Paris. The spire collapsed as crowds watched and prayed, but firefighters saved the cathedral’s structure, and the Crown of Thorns relic was carried to safety.

After five years of restoration by thousands of craftsmen, the cathedral reopened on December 7, 2024, and Mass was celebrated at its new altar the following day, the Solemnity of the Immaculate Conception.

h99.content:
Pope Francis opened a worldwide Synod of Bishops on the theme "For a Synodal Church: Communion, Participation, and Mission" in October 2021. It began with consultations in parishes and dioceses around the world, followed by two assemblies in Rome in October 2023 and October 2024.

For the first time, lay men and women voted alongside bishops as members of the assembly. Pope Francis approved the final document in 2024 as part of his ordinary teaching.

h100.content:
Pope Francis opened the Holy Door of St. Peter’s on Christmas Eve 2024, beginning a Jubilee year with the theme "Pilgrims of Hope." Millions of pilgrims traveled to Rome.

Pope Francis died on Easter Monday, April 21, 2025, in the midst of the Jubilee, and Pope Leo XIV was elected on May 8. During the Jubilee, Leo XIV canonized Sts. Carlo Acutis and Pier Giorgio Frassati on September 7, 2025.

h101.content:
After the Byzantine defeat at Manzikert in 1071, the Seljuk Turks overran most of Asia Minor, and Emperor Alexios I Komnenos appealed to the West for help. In November 1095, at the Council of Clermont in France, Pope Urban II called on Western Christians to aid the Christians of the East and free Jerusalem. The crowd answered, "God wills it!" (Deus vult).

Thousands took the cross. After a long march and the siege of Antioch, the crusaders captured Jerusalem on July 15, 1099, followed by a terrible massacre of its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants. They founded four crusader states: Edessa, Antioch, Tripoli, and the Kingdom of Jerusalem.

h102.content:
The crusades produced a new kind of religious life: knights who took vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience. The Hospitallers grew from a hospital for pilgrims in Jerusalem and were recognized by Pope Paschal II in 1113. Around 1119, Hugues de Payens and a few companions began guarding pilgrims on the roads, and they became the Knights Templar, receiving a rule at the Council of Troyes in 1129. St. Bernard of Clairvaux wrote In Praise of the New Knighthood in their support.

The Teutonic Order began as a German field hospital at the siege of Acre in 1190 and became a military order in 1198. Similar orders arose in Spain and Portugal during the Reconquista.

h103.content:
When the crusader County of Edessa fell in 1144, Pope Eugene III called a new crusade, and St. Bernard of Clairvaux preached it with extraordinary power across France and Germany. King Louis VII of France and King Conrad III of Germany led great armies east.

The campaign was a failure: both armies suffered heavy losses crossing Asia Minor, and their siege of Damascus in 1148 collapsed after a few days. The same year, crusaders on their way by sea helped the Portuguese capture Lisbon.

h104.content:
In 1187 the Muslim sultan Saladin destroyed the army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem at the Horns of Hattin and captured the Holy City in October. The West answered with the Third Crusade, led by Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, who drowned on the way in 1190, King Philip II of France, and King Richard the Lionheart of England.

The crusaders retook Acre in 1191 and won battles along the coast, but never reached Jerusalem. In 1192 Richard and Saladin agreed to a truce that left the city in Muslim hands but allowed Christian pilgrims to visit freely.

h105.content:
The Fourth Crusade never reached the Holy Land. Deep in debt to Venice, the crusaders first attacked the Catholic city of Zara and were excommunicated by Pope Innocent III. They then sailed to Constantinople to restore a deposed Byzantine prince, and in April 1204 they stormed and sacked the greatest Christian city in the world, looting its churches and relics.

Innocent III condemned the sack. The Latin Empire set up in Constantinople lasted until 1261, but the wound to relations between Catholics and Orthodox lasted far longer. In 2001 Pope St. John Paul II asked forgiveness from the Orthodox for the sins of Catholics against them, and in 2004 he expressed his sorrow for the events of 1204 to Patriarch Bartholomew.

h106.content:
In southern France, the Cathars taught that the material world was evil and rejected the sacraments and the Church. St. Dominic preached among them in poverty, but after the murder of a papal legate in 1208, Pope Innocent III called a crusade against them.

The war became a brutal conquest of the south by northern French lords, beginning with the massacre at Béziers in 1209. It ended in 1229, and the struggle against the remaining Cathars led to the creation of the medieval Inquisition.

h107.content:
During the Fifth Crusade, while the crusader army besieged Damietta in Egypt, St. Francis of Assisi crossed the battle lines with Brother Illuminatus to preach the Gospel to Sultan al-Kamil.

The sultan received him courteously, listened to him, and sent him back safely. The encounter became a lasting example of courageous, peaceful witness to Christ, and the Franciscans were later entrusted with the care of the holy places in the Holy Land.

h108.content:
Emperor Frederick II had vowed to go on crusade but delayed so long that Pope Gregory IX excommunicated him. He went anyway, still excommunicated, and instead of fighting he negotiated with Sultan al-Kamil.

By the Treaty of Jaffa in 1229, Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Nazareth were returned to Christian rule without a battle. The city was lost again in 1244, when it was sacked by Khwarazmian forces, and remained under Muslim rule for centuries.

h109.content:
King Louis IX of France, a man of deep personal holiness, led the Seventh Crusade to Egypt in 1248. After early success at Damietta, his army was defeated at Mansurah and the king himself was captured in 1250. He was ransomed and spent four years strengthening the defenses of the crusader states.

In 1270 he set out again, landing at Tunis, where disease swept through the camp. Louis died there on August 25, 1270, and was canonized in 1297.

h110.content:
After nearly two centuries, the last great crusader stronghold, Acre, fell to the Mamluk sultan al-Ashraf Khalil in May 1291 after a six-week siege. The Templars and Hospitallers fought to the end, and many defenders and citizens were killed or enslaved.

The remaining coastal towns were abandoned within months, ending the crusader states in the Holy Land. The military orders withdrew to Cyprus, and later to Rhodes and Malta.

h111.content:
For nearly eight centuries after the Muslim conquest of 711, the Christian kingdoms of northern Spain slowly pushed south. The popes granted the struggle the status of a crusade, and Spanish military orders such as Calatrava and Santiago fought in it.

The decisive victory came at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212, when the kings of Castile, Aragon, and Navarre defeated the Almohad army. The Reconquista was completed when Ferdinand and Isabella took Granada in January 1492.

h112.content:
On Friday, October 13, 1307, King Philip IV of France, who owed the Templars large sums, had every Templar in France arrested on charges of heresy and blasphemy. Many confessed under torture, and some later retracted.

Under heavy pressure from the king, Pope Clement V suppressed the order at the Council of Vienne in 1312 without condemning it as heretical, and gave most of its property to the Hospitallers. The last Grand Master, Jacques de Molay, was burned in Paris in 1314. A document found in the Vatican archives in 2001, the Chinon Parchment, shows that the pope had absolved the leaders in 1308.

h113.content:
In the thirteenth century, popes authorized crusades against the pagan peoples of the Baltic. The Teutonic Order conquered Prussia and, with the Livonian Order, much of today’s Latvia and Estonia, creating a powerful monastic state.

Lithuania, the last pagan state in Europe, accepted Christianity through the marriage of Grand Duke Jogaila to St. Jadwiga of Poland in 1386. In 1410 the united Polish and Lithuanian army crushed the Teutonic Knights at the Battle of Grunwald (Tannenberg).

h114.content:
In 1565 the Ottoman sultan Suleiman the Magnificent sent a great fleet and army against Malta, held by the Knights Hospitaller under Grand Master Jean de la Valette. For nearly four months a few hundred knights and several thousand soldiers and Maltese defended the island against an army many times larger.

Fort St. Elmo fell after a heroic defense, but the other forts held, and the Ottomans withdrew in September when relief arrived from Sicily. The new capital of Malta was named Valletta in honor of the Grand Master.

h115.content:
In 1683 a huge Ottoman army besieged Vienna, capital of the Holy Roman Empire. Pope Bl. Innocent XI worked tirelessly to unite the Christian princes, and King Jan III Sobieski of Poland led a relief army.

On September 12, 1683, the combined Christian armies, led by Sobieski’s famous winged hussars, broke the siege. In thanksgiving, Innocent XI extended the feast of the Holy Name of Mary to the whole Church, and it is kept on September 12.

h116.content:
On the First Sunday of Lent in the Great Jubilee of 2000, Pope St. John Paul II led a solemn liturgy in St. Peter’s Basilica asking God’s forgiveness for sins committed by the Church’s members over the centuries.

The prayers confessed sins against the unity of Christians, the use of violence in the service of truth, sins against the Jewish people, against the dignity of women and of peoples, and against the poor. The Church, the Pope taught, is holy, but her members are sinners who must always repent and purify memory.

h117.content:
In seventh-century Northumbria, Christians trained by Irish monks and those formed in the Roman tradition kept Easter on different dates, so that the king and queen sometimes celebrated it in different weeks.

At the Synod of Whitby, held at the abbey of St. Hilda, King Oswiu heard both sides and decided for the Roman reckoning, because St. Peter held the keys of the kingdom. The decision drew the English Church more closely into the life of the whole Western Church.

h118.content:
A century after the death of Muhammad, Umayyad armies had conquered North Africa and Spain and crossed the Pyrenees into Gaul. In October 732 the Frankish leader Charles Martel defeated them between Tours and Poitiers.

The battle halted the Muslim advance into northern Europe. Charles’s grandson was Charlemagne, who would be crowned emperor in 800.

h119.content:
In 966 Duke Mieszko I, ruler of the Polans, was baptized, bringing his people into the Christian West. His marriage to the Christian princess Dobrawa of Bohemia helped prepare the way.

Poland celebrates its baptism as the birth of the nation. In 2016 Poland marked its 1,050th anniversary, and the faith of this people later gave the Church Pope St. John Paul II.

h120.content:
In 1595 most of the Orthodox bishops of the Kyivan Metropolia, in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, sent representatives to Rome and entered into full communion with the Pope, keeping their Byzantine liturgy, calendar, and married clergy. The union was proclaimed at Brest in 1596.

It was bitterly opposed by many Orthodox, and St. Josaphat Kuntsevych was martyred in 1623 for his work for unity. The Ukrainian and Belarusian Greek Catholic Churches trace their communion with Rome to this union.
